comments.text:
Hi Dr Mike. I'm a professional filmmaker who worked on 3 Seasons of the Good Doctor. I'm also a trained lifeguard and mountain rescue guild who has performed CPR in the field before.

The reason that the CPR in shows is so poor looking is a budgetary issue. Obviously you can't perform real chest compressions on a healthy individual, so you're left with two options. Digital effects in post, or a prosthetic/mannequin. 

For digital effects, it would be surprisingly time consuming and expensive to plan and execute your filming in a way that could than be manipulated in post, and most hospital shows do not have a VFX team that size. For a show which is shot so naturistically like the Pitt (so I hear) it would also be disruptive to the flow of set and the Actors and Directors.

For prosthetics, shows like the Pitt already have an amazing team of effects artists working around the clock to produce the amazing pieces we see. To also produce prosthetics for every person who receives CPR would balloon the budget and time constraints of a team already working around the clock, and would most likely double their production times and budget. realistically we're all in contention with the funding of our shows, and concessions have to be made here and there.

A easier option that shows could adopt is simply not showing the chest during compressions, but that might feel strange to never see certain angles while CPR is being performed.

I absolutely agree with you, the CPR looks silly, but hopefully we can suspend our disbelief along with the other dramatizations of protocol and behavior, and forgive the Pitt for it's transgressions. Love your content, love hearing about all the medicine underpinning a great show like the Pitt.

comments.text:
About the ASL interpretation:  anyone in medicine reading this, please only communicate directly with the patient in writing or through the asl interpreter provided by the hospital.  Don’t assume signing family members are relaying your communications accurately.  Probably goes for foreign languages as well.

Story time: my next door neighbors were a lovely elderly deaf couple. They were also taking care of the wife’s 90-something mother.  The wife had beat back cancer a couple of times, but it came back.  The wife’s mother (hearing) called me to try to do some palliative soft tissue therapy to help her daughter with the pain she was experiencing.  I walked in and immediately recognized that she should have been on hospice.  Found out they  stopped her chemo because it wasn’t working anymore.  But the mother told the patient that it was so she could “get strong enough to continue treatment.”  She, understandably, didn’t want her daughter to give up.  She was hoping for a miracle.  And thought, inaccurately, that if she was put on hospice, THAT was the death sentence because you aren’t allowed to come off it.  So the mother lied about what the doctor was saying, and the doctor just treated the mother like an unbiased interpreter.  While what I did was helpful, what this meant was that the wife had been managing her end-of-life, late stage cancer levels of pain as parts of her extremities were seeping as her organs died…with Tylenol.  For weeks.  I begged the mother to tell the wife and get going on hospice, but she couldn’t bring herself to do so for way too long, and it would be out of my ethical scope of practice to do it myself.  NO ONE TOLD THIS COUPLE THAT SHE WAS DYING .  And I’m upset that the mother didn’t relay the information truthfully, but I understand the gravity of her situation.  I’m far more mad at the doctors that didn’t follow good communication protocol to make sure she was able to make the best decisions she could for herself.  They allowed the wife’s mother to take her autonomy away and make dignified decisions about her end of life care and pain management for herself.  No evil malice to it, of course.  Likely the opposite.  But because of it, the woman was in terrible pain for months.  I had finally decided I couldn’t watch it anymore and was going to tell her, when the mother called and finally asked me to help her navigate getting in touch with hospice.  She was on comfort care for less than a day before she passed.  I genuinely believe she was in too much pain to let go until then.  

So please…PLEASE be mindful of this, providers, when there’s a family member “interpreting.”  You need a real interpreter.  Or you need, in the case of ASL, to write directly to the patient if a signing interpreter isn’t available.
